items.stem: A company runs a production application on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The application stores customer orders in one Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance, and analysts run long reporting queries against the same DB instance every month. The database must keep accepting writes, without losing committed data, if its Availability Zone fails. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: keep accepting writes, without losing committed data

options.text: Run PostgreSQL on two EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, with replication and failover that the team manages, and reports on the second instance.
options.why: It can work, but on EC2 the team owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the failover itself.
options.misconception: runs the database on instances for control, which adds operating work that RDS removes

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and keep sending every query to the existing DB instance endpoint.
options.why: A Multi-AZ DB instance protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption), with [automatic failover to standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and send the reporting queries to the standby DB instance in the second Availability Zone.
options.why: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the reporting part of this design cannot work.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance in a second Availability Zone, and send the reporting queries to the read replica endpoint.
options.why: A read replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote), and for write availability AWS advises to [run your DB instance as a Multi-AZ deployment](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multi-az-for-write-availability).

items.explanation: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, database writes are [concurrent on the primary and standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous), so the standby holds every committed write. On a zone failure, RDS fails over and keeps the [name record for your DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-automatic-failover). The team turns it on [by modifying the DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-convert-by-modifying) and runs no failover process.
items.takeaway: Zone failure with no lost writes: Multi-AZ. Reports that slow the primary: a read replica.
items.twin: If the stem said "The reporting queries must stop slowing down the order writes on the primary DB instance" instead: the read replica, because it serves [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition).
items.say: A zone failure with no lost writes points to Multi-AZ, because the standby gets every write at the same time.

solvers.stem_only: Convert the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment: a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover keeps writes going without losing committed data. The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance serves no reads, so the reporting detail is a distractor; the application keeps using the same endpoint.

items.stem: A company runs an order database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Automated backups are turned on, with a backup retention period of 7 days. The company has no manual DB snapshots. Two hours ago, an engineer deleted a table by mistake. The company must recover the table as it was at a specific time, 5 minutes before the deletion. What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

options.text: Rely on the standby DB instance of the Multi-AZ deployment, which keeps a second copy of all of the data in another Availability Zone.
options.why: Writes are [concurrent on the primary and standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous), so the standby lost the table at the same moment as the primary.

options.text: Roll back the existing DB instance in place to an earlier point in time, so that the application can keep using the same endpoint.
options.why: RDS restores by [creating a new DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention), which is [created with a new endpoint](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-restore-creates-new-instance); the existing DB instance stays as it is.

options.text: Restore the database to a point in time as a new DB instance, copy back the needed data, and delete the new instance.
options.why: A restore can reach [any second during your retention period](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-pitr-any-second-latest-restorable), and two hours ago is inside the 7 days, so the table comes back on the new DB instance.

options.text: Take a manual DB snapshot of the DB instance now, and keep the snapshot until the company decides to delete it.
options.why: A snapshot taken now holds the database after the deletion, so the deleted table is missing from it.
options.misconception: a new snapshot can bring back data that was deleted before the snapshot

items.explanation: Automated backups enable [point-in-time recovery](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-automated-backups-enable-pitr): RDS keeps a daily snapshot and the transaction logs. So RDS can recover [any point in time](../facts/rds.md#rds-automated-backup-pitr-in-retention) inside the 7-day retention period. The restore creates a new DB instance, and the team copies the table back from it.
items.takeaway: Undo a recent mistake: a point-in-time restore to a new DB instance. Keep a copy for years: a manual snapshot.
items.twin: If the stem said "retain a copy of the database as it is today for 7 years" instead: the manual snapshot, because manual snapshots are [kept until you explicitly delete them](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-snapshots-user-initiated-kept-until-deleted).
items.say: A recent mistake inside the retention period calls for a point-in-time restore to a new DB instance.

solvers.stem_only: Use point-in-time recovery from the automated backups to a time 5 minutes before the deletion. RDS restores to a NEW DB instance (no in-place rollback for RDS for MySQL); then copy the table back to production and delete the temporary instance. The Multi-AZ standby replicated the deletion too.

items.stem: A web application on Amazon EC2 instances connects to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. During a failover test, the application lost all its open database connections, and some clients kept using the old IP address of the database for several minutes. The company wants minimal downtime during future failovers, and it accepts only minimal code changes. Which solution will BEST meet these requirements?
keywords: lost all its open database connections
kept using the old IP address

options.text: Make no change, because the DB instance endpoint name stays the same after a failover and the open connections move to the standby.
options.why: At failover RDS [changes the Domain Name System (DNS) record](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-failover-dns-change-reconnect), and the application must [re-establish any existing connections](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-failover-dns-change-reconnect).

options.text: Add connection retry logic to every application component, and lower the DNS cache time to live on every EC2 instance to a few seconds.
options.why: AWS advises to [implement database connection retry at the application layer](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cname-flip-retry), but this changes code in every component and still drops each open connection.
options.misconception: rewrites every component when a managed proxy keeps the connections

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS Proxy for the DB instance, and change the database endpoint in the application configuration to the proxy endpoint.
options.why: The proxy accepts connections [at the same IP address](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-failover-same-ip-no-dns) and [directs connections to the new primary](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-failover-same-ip-no-dns), with [no code changes](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-faq-no-code-changes) for most applications.

options.text: Create a read replica in a second Availability Zone, and send the application's writes to the read replica while a failover runs.
options.why: Clients have [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only), and RDS does not allow a PostgreSQL read replica [to be made writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-postgresql-not-writable).

items.explanation: RDS Proxy [bypasses Domain Name System (DNS) caches](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-faq-bypasses-dns-caches) and reduces failover times by [up to 66%](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-failover-66-percent) for Multi-AZ DB instances. Through the proxy, [most connections stay alive during failovers](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-failover-idle-connections-kept). The application changes one endpoint setting.
items.takeaway: Failover drops connections and DNS caches lag: put RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application must keep connecting directly to the database" instead: retry logic and a DNS cache time to live of [less than 30 seconds](../facts/rds.md#rds-bp-dns-ttl-under-30-seconds).
items.say: Put RDS Proxy in front of the database: it keeps the client connections and sends them to the new primary.

solvers.stem_only: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance and point the application at the proxy endpoint. The proxy holds client connections, routes to the new primary after failover without waiting for DNS propagation, and shortens failover time; only a configuration change is needed.

items.stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for MariaDB DB instance in a single Availability Zone. A reporting team wants its own copy of the data to query. When an administrator tries to create a read replica of the DB instance, RDS refuses the request. The DB instance uses a general-purpose instance class, and its backup retention period is set to 0. What should the administrator do first to create the read replica?
keywords: backup retention period is set to 0

options.text: Convert the source DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, because RDS creates read replicas from the standby.
options.why: A Single-AZ source works and sees an I/O pause of [about one second](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-create-io-suspension); the retention period of 0 is what blocks the request.

options.text: Take a manual DB snapshot of the source DB instance, and create the read replica from that manual snapshot.
options.why: RDS [takes a snapshot of the source instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-created-from-snapshot) itself when it creates a replica, and a manual snapshot does not turn on automated backups.
options.misconception: a read replica is created from a manual snapshot that the administrator takes

options.text: Modify the source DB instance to a larger memory-optimized instance class, and then retry the creation of the read replica.
options.why: The class is not the cause: before a replica you must [enable automatic backups on the source DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-requires-automated-backups).
options.misconception: the size of the source instance blocks the creation of a read replica

options.text: Set the backup retention period of the source DB instance to more than 0, which turns on automated backups.
options.why: The source of a read replica needs a backup retention period of [a value other than 0](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-requires-automated-backups), which turns on automated backups.

items.explanation: A retention period of 0 means no automated backups: [Setting the backup retention period to 0 disables automated backups](../facts/rds.md#rds-backup-retention-range). A read replica needs automated backups on its source, and [Backups must remain enabled](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-read-replica-needs-backups) while the replica exists. After the change, RDS can create the replica.
items.takeaway: No automated backups on the source means no read replica: set a retention period above 0 first.
items.twin: If the stem said "its backup retention period is set to 7 days" instead: create the read replica directly, because the source already has automated backups.
items.say: A read replica needs automated backups on its source, so set the retention period above zero first.

solvers.stem_only: A read replica requires automated backups on the source. A backup retention period of 0 turns them off, so set the retention period to a value greater than 0 first, then create the replica.

items.stem: A company runs a production application on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The application stores customer orders in one Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance, and analysts run long reporting queries against the same DB instance every month. The reporting queries must stop slowing down the order writes on the primary DB instance. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: reporting queries must stop slowing down the order writes

options.text: Run PostgreSQL on two EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, with replication and failover that the team manages, and reports on the second instance.
options.why: It can work, but on EC2 the team owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the replication itself.
options.misconception: runs the database on instances for control, which adds operating work that RDS removes

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and keep sending every query to the existing DB instance endpoint.
options.why: A Multi-AZ DB instance [isn't a scaling solution for read-only scenarios](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-not-read-scaling), so the reports still run on the primary.

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and send the reporting queries to the standby DB instance in the second Availability Zone.
options.why: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the reports cannot move to it.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance in a second Availability Zone, and send the reporting queries to the read replica endpoint.
options.why: A read replica serves [business reporting or data warehousing scenarios](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-use-reporting) on its own endpoint, so the reports leave the primary.

items.explanation: A read replica is a [read-only copy of a DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition). RDS takes the updates of the primary and [copies them asynchronously to the read replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only). The reporting queries move to the replica endpoint, and the primary keeps its capacity for the order writes. RDS creates and maintains the replica, so the team runs no replication software.
items.takeaway: Reports that slow the primary: a read replica. A Multi-AZ DB instance standby serves no reads.
items.twin: If the stem said "The database must keep accepting writes, without losing committed data, if its Availability Zone fails" instead: Multi-AZ, which protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption).
items.say: Reporting that slows the primary points to a read replica, because the Multi-AZ standby serves no reads.

solvers.stem_only: Create a read replica (asynchronous replication) and send the reporting queries to the replica endpoint, which offloads reads from the primary. A Multi-AZ DB instance standby cannot serve reads, and self-managed EC2 adds overhead.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on three Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone. The application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the same Availability Zone. The company must make the application highly available, so that it keeps working if one Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Launch three more EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone, and put an Application Load Balancer in front of all six instances.
options.why: Every instance stays in the zone that can fail, and an Application Load Balancer needs [at least two Availability Zone subnets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-subnets-two-azs-different).

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group that launches the instances across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer.
options.why: With two zones, the [desired capacity is distributed across these Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-desired-spread-across-azs), so instances keep running when one zone fails.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance in the same Availability Zone, and point the application to the replica if the primary fails.
options.why: The replica sits in the same zone, and a replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote) instead of failing over by itself.

options.text: Install MySQL on an EC2 instance in a second Availability Zone, and run replication and failover scripts that the team maintains.
options.why: It can work, but the team then owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the failover scripts.
options.misconception: builds its own standby database when RDS offers a managed one

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that RDS keeps a synchronous standby in a second Availability Zone.
options.why: RDS keeps a [synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads) and has [automatic failover to standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).

items.explanation: Both tiers sit in the zone that can fail, so both need a second zone. EC2 Auto Scaling [maintains balance across all of the Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-desired-spread-across-azs) of the group. A Multi-AZ DB instance protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption), and RDS runs the failover.
items.takeaway: High availability puts every tier in two zones: an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer, and Multi-AZ RDS.
items.twin: If the stem said "if the whole AWS Region fails" instead: a copy in a second Region, such as a cross-Region read replica, which stays available [if one Region becomes unavailable](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-region-async-replica-survives-region).
items.say: Both tiers need a second zone: an Auto Scaling group across two zones, and a Multi-AZ database.

solvers.stem_only: Two layers must survive an AZ failure: the web tier (Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs behind an Application Load Balancer) and the database (Multi-AZ deployment with a synchronous standby and automatic failover).

items.stem: A company runs an order service on a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company needs automatic failover that typically completes in under a minute if the primary fails. The company also wants the standby capacity to serve the dashboard read queries through a separate read-only endpoint, so that the dashboards stop loading the primary. Which deployment option will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
keywords: standby capacity to serve the dashboard read queries

options.text: Deploy a Multi-AZ DB cluster, send the writes to its writer endpoint, and send the dashboard queries to its reader endpoint.
options.why: The cluster's readers [act as automatic failover targets](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-native-replication-failover-target), failover typically takes [under 35 seconds](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-failover-time), and the [reader endpoint](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-writer-reader-endpoints) serves the dashboards.

options.text: Deploy a Multi-AZ DB instance, and send the dashboard queries to the standby DB instance in the second Availability Zone.
options.why: The standby [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), and its failover typically takes [60–120 seconds](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-failover-time).

options.text: Keep the Single-AZ DB instance, add two read replicas for the dashboards, and run a script that promotes a replica on failure.
options.why: A replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote), and promotion takes [several minutes or longer](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-promote-reboot-minutes), so the failover is slow.

options.text: Run PostgreSQL on three EC2 instances in three Availability Zones, with replication, failover and a read-only endpoint that the team manages.
options.why: It can work, but on EC2 the team owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the failover design.
options.misconception: builds its own cluster when RDS offers a managed one

items.explanation: A Multi-AZ DB cluster runs a writer and [two reader DB instances](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read) in [three separate Availability Zones](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read), and [all three DB instances can serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read). RDS runs the replication and the failover, so the cluster meets both needs as a managed option.
items.takeaway: Fast failover plus readable standbys on MySQL or PostgreSQL: a Multi-AZ DB cluster.
items.twin: If the stem said "failover within a few minutes, and the dashboards can stay on the primary" instead: a Multi-AZ DB instance, with failover in [60–120 seconds](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-failover-time).
items.say: Fast failover and standbys that serve reads point to a Multi-AZ DB cluster.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the deployment option that is MOST operationally efficient.
I mark the constraints: RDS for PostgreSQL, automatic failover that typically finishes in under a minute, and standby capacity that serves the dashboard reads through a separate endpoint.

Before I look at the options, I predict a Multi-AZ DB cluster, because its two reader DB instances are automatic failover targets that also serve reads, and its failover typically takes under 35 seconds.

I remove the Multi-AZ DB instance, because its standby serves no reads and its failover typically takes 60 to 120 seconds. I remove the read replicas with a script, because a replica is promoted manually and promotion takes several minutes or longer.

Between the Multi-AZ DB cluster and PostgreSQL on EC2 the difference is who runs the replication and the failover; the stem says MOST operationally efficient, so the managed cluster wins over a design that the team builds and operates.
Check: the Multi-AZ DB cluster runs on PostgreSQL, fails over automatically in under a minute, serves the dashboards from its reader endpoint and needs no scripts. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment (one writer, two readable standbys in three AZs): failover typically under a minute, plus a reader endpoint that serves read-only queries from the standbys. A Multi-AZ DB instance standby is not readable.

items.stem: A company runs an order database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Automated backups are turned on, with a backup retention period of 7 days. The company has no manual DB snapshots. A new regulation mandates that the company retain a copy of the database as it is today for 7 years. What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?
keywords: retain a copy of the database as it is today

options.text: Rely on the standby DB instance of the Multi-AZ deployment, which keeps a second copy of all of the data in another Availability Zone.
options.why: The standby changes with every write, because writes are [concurrent on the primary and standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous), so it keeps no copy of the database as it is today.

options.text: Roll back the existing DB instance in place to an earlier point in time, so that the application can keep using the same endpoint.
options.why: RDS restores by [creating a new DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention), not by a rollback in place, and a rollback would keep no copy for 7 years.

options.text: Restore the database to a point in time as a new DB instance, copy back the needed data, and delete the new instance.
options.why: The new DB instance is deleted at the end, so nothing is kept, and automated backups are kept for [between 0 and 35 days](../facts/rds.md#rds-backup-retention-range).
options.misconception: a short-term restore also keeps a long-term copy

options.text: Take a manual DB snapshot of the DB instance now, and keep the snapshot until the company decides to delete it.
options.why: Manual snapshots [aren't subject to the backup retention period](../facts/rds.md#rds-manual-snapshots-dont-expire), so the copy of today's database stays until the company deletes it.

items.explanation: Manual DB snapshots are [kept until you explicitly delete them](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-snapshots-user-initiated-kept-until-deleted), while automated backups last [between 0 and 35 days](../facts/rds.md#rds-backup-retention-range). A snapshot taken now holds the database as it is today, and it outlives the 7-day automated backups, so it meets the regulation.
items.takeaway: Keep a copy for years: a manual snapshot. Automated backups expire with their retention period.
items.twin: If the stem said "Two hours ago, an engineer deleted a table by mistake" instead: the point-in-time restore to a new DB instance, which reaches [any second during your retention period](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-pitr-any-second-latest-restorable).
items.say: A copy to keep for years is a manual snapshot, because manual snapshots do not expire.

solvers.stem_only: Automated backups expire with the retention period (at most 35 days), so take a manual DB snapshot now; manual snapshots stay until someone deletes them, which covers 7 years. (AWS Backup with a 7-year rule would also work, if offered.)

items.stem: A company runs a mission-critical transactional (OLTP) database on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The DB instance uses a general-purpose instance class and General Purpose SSD (gp3) storage. At peak, the workload performs many small random writes, and commit times vary with the storage response time. The company needs consistent, low storage latency for this workload. Which storage configuration will provide the LOWEST latency for the database storage?

options.text: Keep General Purpose SSD (gp3) storage, and turn on storage autoscaling so that RDS adds storage before each peak.
options.why: When free space runs low, [it automatically scales up your storage](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable), but gp3 latency stays [single-digit millisecond, provided consistently 99% of the time](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-latency-by-type).
options.misconception: storage autoscaling makes the storage faster

options.text: Move the storage to a larger General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume, so that the baseline IOPS grow with the volume size.
options.why: The gp2 baseline grows at [3 IOPS for each GiB](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-gp2-baseline-per-gib), but its latency stays [single-digit millisecond, provided consistently 99% of the time](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-latency-by-type).

options.text: Move the storage to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express), and provision the IOPS rate that the peak workload needs.
options.why: io2 Block Express gives [sub-millisecond, provided consistently 99.9% of the time](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-latency-by-type) latency, and Provisioned IOPS fits [high-performance OLTP workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-choice-oltp-moderate).

options.text: Change the DB instance to a memory-optimized instance class, and keep the General Purpose SSD (gp3) storage as it is.
options.why: More memory helps reads when the working set [resides almost completely in memory](../facts/rds.md#rds-bp-working-set-in-memory), but each commit still waits for the gp3 storage.
options.misconception: more memory lowers the latency of storage writes

items.explanation: Provisioned IOPS storage is built for [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production). Each commit waits for the storage, so the storage type sets the commit time. More memory or more capacity leaves the gp3 latency class as it is.
items.takeaway: Consistent sub-millisecond storage latency for OLTP: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express).
items.twin: If the stem said "a development database with moderate I/O and a small budget" instead: General Purpose SSD (gp3), which is [best suited for development and testing environments](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-gp-for-dev-test).
items.say: Consistent low storage latency for OLTP points to Provisioned IOPS on io2 Block Express.

solvers.stem_only: Move to Provisioned IOPS SSD storage, specifically io2 Block Express, which gives consistent sub-millisecond latency for I/O-intensive OLTP, and provision the IOPS for peak. Instance class, gp2 size or storage autoscaling do not fix storage latency.

items.stem: A company runs a production database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. The company must upgrade the database to a new major engine version. Before the switch, the team wants to test the new version on a copy of the database that stays in sync with production. The switch must cause minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Upgrade the engine version in place, because the Multi-AZ deployment upgrades the standby first and then fails over to it.
options.why: An engine upgrade [modifies both primary and secondary DB instances](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-engine-upgrade-both-down), and it [causes downtime until the upgrade is complete](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-engine-upgrade-both-down).

options.text: Take a DB snapshot, restore it to a new DB instance, upgrade the new DB instance, and move the application to it.
options.why: A copy made by [restoring from the DB snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-test-upgrade-on-restored-copy) is good for a test, but it receives no production writes after the snapshot.
options.misconception: a copy restored from a snapshot stays in sync with production

options.text: Use AWS Database Migration Service to replicate the data to a new DB instance on the new version, test it, and then cut over.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds, runs and cuts over the replication itself, which a blue/green deployment does for the team.
options.misconception: builds its own replication for an upgrade that RDS can stage

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployment, upgrade the green environment to the new version, test it, and then switch over.
options.why: The green environment [stays in sync with the current production environment](../facts/rds.md#rds-blue-green-staging-in-sync), and blue/green deployments suit [major or minor version database engine upgrades](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-blue-green-use-cases).

items.explanation: An engine upgrade needs downtime, [even for Multi-AZ instances](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-upgrade-downtime-even-multiaz), and AWS advises to minimize it by [using a blue/green deployment](../facts/rds.md#rds-engine-upgrade-downtime-blue-green). The switch has [short, predictable downtime](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-blue-green-use-cases), and RDS keeps the green copy in sync, so the team runs no replication of its own.
items.takeaway: Major upgrade, tested on a synced copy, short switch: an RDS Blue/Green Deployment.
items.twin: If the stem said "a minor engine version, and a short outage in the maintenance window is acceptable" instead: an in-place upgrade with [Auto Minor Version Upgrade](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-auto-minor-version-upgrade).
items.say: A major upgrade tested on a synced copy with a short switch points to a Blue/Green Deployment.

solvers.stem_only: Use Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments: RDS creates a green copy kept in sync by logical replication, you upgrade and test the green environment, then switch over, usually in about a minute. An in-place Multi-AZ upgrade upgrades both primary and standby together and causes downtime.

items.stem: A development team uses an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance for testing from 08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays. The schedule is predictable, and nobody uses the DB instance at night or on weekends. The data in the database must stay between working days, and the team wants no manual steps each day. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: nobody uses the DB instance at night or on weekends
The data in the database must stay

options.text: Stop the DB instance every Friday evening and start it every Monday morning, and keep it running on weekday nights.
options.why: It removes the weekend hours. A stopped DB instance is billed for storage [but not for DB instance hours](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-billing-stopped-instance), and this design still pays for every weekday night.
options.misconception: stopping the DB instance at weekends removes most of the idle cost

options.text: Use an automated schedule that stops the DB instance every evening and starts it again every working morning.
options.why: While it is stopped, [you're not charged for DB instance hours](../facts/rds.md#rds-stop-billing), and each stop lasts far less than [7 consecutive days](../facts/rds.md#rds-stop-max-seven-days).

options.text: Buy a three-year Reserved DB instance for the instance class, and keep the DB instance running all day, every day.
options.why: A reservation is a [one or three year term](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-ri-terms-one-or-three-year) commitment that pays for every hour, but this DB instance is idle most hours of each week.
options.misconception: a commitment discount is cheaper than stopping an instance that is idle most of the week

options.text: Delete the DB instance every evening without a final snapshot, and restore it every morning from its automated backups.
options.why: Without a final snapshot, [all automated backups are deleted](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-instance-automated-backups-deleted) with the DB instance, so nothing is left to restore in the morning.

items.explanation: The DB instance is idle every night and every weekend. RDS bills a stopped DB instance for storage [but not for DB instance hours](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-billing-stopped-instance), so a daily stop and start removes the instance cost of every idle period. A schedule does this with no manual steps, and the data stays in the stopped DB instance.
items.takeaway: Idle every night and weekend on a known schedule: stop and start the DB instance automatically.
items.twin: If the stem said "the database serves production traffic all day, every day" instead: a Reserved DB instance, a [one or three year term](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-ri-terms-one-or-three-year) commitment for steady use.
items.say: A database that sits idle every night should be stopped on a schedule, because a stopped instance pays no instance hours.

solvers.stem_only: Stop the DB instance outside working hours and start it each working morning on an automated schedule (for example EventBridge Scheduler or Instance Scheduler on AWS). A stopped instance keeps its data and you pay only for storage; daily stops stay well inside the 7-day auto-start limit.

items.stem: A company runs a latency-sensitive application on two Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads and writes orders through its own pool of 20 long-lived connections to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The number of connections stays far below the limit of the DB instance. An architect proposes Amazon RDS Proxy for every database of the company. The application needs low latency for every query. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: its own pool of 20 long-lived connections

options.text: Keep the application connected directly to the DB instance endpoint, and keep using the connection pool of the application.
options.why: The application already pools its connections, so a direct connection avoids the average of [5 milliseconds](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-faq-adds-5-ms-connect-directly) that a proxy can add, and the proxy charge.

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, because every RDS database needs a proxy to pool its connections.
options.why: A proxy would work, but it is [priced per vCPU per hour](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-pricing-per-vcpu) and adds latency for an application that already pools.

options.text: Move the application to AWS Lambda functions that open a new database connection in each invocation, and remove the EC2 instances.
options.why: Many concurrent functions can [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy), and a new connection for each invocation adds setup time to each request.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance, and move the connection pool of the application to the read replica endpoint.
options.why: The application also writes orders, and clients have [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only); the replica is also a second DB instance to pay for.

items.explanation: RDS Proxy helps applications that [don't have built-in connection pooling mechanisms](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-candidate-no-builtin-pool). This application already keeps its own pool far below the connection limit. AWS notes that the proxy can add [5 milliseconds](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-faq-adds-5-ms-connect-directly) on average, so an application that needs no connection management can connect directly.
items.takeaway: An application with its own pool and few connections connects directly; RDS Proxy would add cost and latency.
items.twin: If the stem said "thousands of short-lived Lambda invocations open new connections" instead: RDS Proxy, because functions make [frequent short database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling).
items.say: This application already pools its connections, so it connects directly and avoids the proxy's latency and cost.

solvers.stem_only: Change nothing: the application already pools a small, steady number of long-lived connections far below the limit, so RDS Proxy adds cost and a network hop (extra latency) with no benefit. Keep the direct connection.

verification.note: exam-10: three weak distractors for a difficulty 3 item; replaced in the shipped set by the verified difficulty 3 question rds-q022

items.stem: A company's web application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to fix a performance problem without any change to the application's SQL queries. During spiky traffic, thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections, and the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections
too many connections errors at low CPU use

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to use the proxy endpoint.
options.why: Lambda functions make [frequent short database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling), and the proxy keeps a [smaller number of long-lived connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections) open to the database.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to send its read-only queries to the replica.
options.why: A replica takes reads, but each Lambda environment still opens its own connection, and high concurrency can [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy) again.
options.misconception: a second DB instance fixes a storm of short-lived connections

options.text: Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances, and run a connection pooler and streaming read replicas that the team manages.
options.why: A self-managed pooler works, but on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) of the database.
options.misconception: builds connection pooling by hand when a managed proxy exists

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby instance also serves part of the query load.
options.why: The standby [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), and a Multi-AZ deployment does not pool the connections of the functions.

items.explanation: The errors come from the number of connections, not from CPU. Lambda functions benefit from the [connection pooling offered by RDS Proxy](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling). With multiplexing, the proxy [keeps a smaller number of connections open](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-multiplexing-fewer-db-connections) to the DB instance, so the connection errors become less likely without a larger instance.
items.takeaway: Connection errors at low CPU point to RDS Proxy; heavy reads point to a read replica.
items.twin: If the stem said "Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent at peak, but the number of database connections stays low" instead: a read replica, because it serves [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition).
items.say: The database is out of connections, not CPU, so I'd put RDS Proxy in front to pool them.

solvers.stem_only: Too many connections at low CPU from many short-lived Lambda invocations is the classic RDS Proxy case: the proxy pools and shares connections. Only the connection endpoint changes, not the SQL.

items.stem: An audit finds that a company's Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance was created without encryption. The company must encrypt the data at rest with an AWS KMS key, and the encryption must also cover the automated backups and any future read replicas. A short maintenance window for the cutover is acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: encrypt the data at rest with an AWS KMS key

options.text: Modify the DB instance to turn on encryption with the KMS key, and apply the change during the next maintenance window.
options.why: You can [only encrypt an Amazon RDS DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create) when you create it, so a modification cannot turn encryption on.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance that is encrypted with the KMS key, and promote the replica to a standalone DB instance.
options.why: For an encrypted read replica, [the source DB instance must be encrypted](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-encrypted-needs-encrypted-source), and this source is not encrypted.

options.text: Take a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption under the KMS key, and restore a new DB instance from the encrypted copy.
options.why: RDS lets you [encrypt a copy of an unencrypted snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy) and [restore an encrypted DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy) from that copy, with a short cutover.

options.text: Create a new encrypted DB instance with the KMS key, and move the data with a dump and restore that the team scripts and runs.
options.why: It works, but the team writes, tests and runs the dump and the restore, which a snapshot copy does without scripts.
options.misconception: moves the data by hand when an encrypted snapshot copy does it

items.explanation: RDS encrypts a DB instance at creation, [not after the DB instance is created](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create), so the fix is a new, encrypted DB instance. An encrypted snapshot copy creates it without scripts. After the restore, encryption covers the [logs, automated backups, read replicas, and snapshots](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-at-rest-scope). The application moves to the new endpoint in the maintenance window.
items.takeaway: To encrypt an existing DB instance, copy a snapshot with encryption and restore a new DB instance.
items.twin: If the stem said "a DB instance that the company will create next month" instead: turn on encryption at creation, because RDS encrypts a DB instance then and [not after the DB instance is created](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create).
items.say: Encryption is set at creation, so I'd copy a snapshot with the KMS key and restore from it.

solvers.stem_only: Encryption cannot be turned on for an existing unencrypted DB instance, and an encrypted read replica cannot be made from an unencrypted source. Take a snapshot, copy it with encryption under the KMS key, restore a new encrypted DB instance from the copy, and cut over; its backups and replicas are then encrypted.

items.stem: A company is moving a legacy packaged application from its data center to AWS. The application uses a Microsoft SQL Server database. The software vendor supports the application only when the vendor's monitoring agent runs on the operating system of the database host. The company wants AWS to automate as much database administration as possible, such as backups and patching. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: agent runs on the operating system of the database host
automate as much database administration as possible

options.text: Run the database on Amazon RDS for SQL Server, and install the vendor's agent on the host of the DB instance.
options.why: Standard Amazon RDS [doesn't let you access the underlying host](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-os-access), so the vendor's agent has no place to run.

options.text: Run SQL Server on Amazon EC2 instances that the team manages, and install the vendor's agent on each instance.
options.why: It works, but with SQL Server on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks).
options.misconception: takes full control of the host when a managed option gives the access that is needed

options.text: Move the database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, and run the vendor's agent on an EC2 instance next to the cluster.
options.why: The packaged application is built for SQL Server, and an agent on a separate EC2 instance is not on the database host.
options.misconception: changes the engine of a packaged application and places the agent away from the database host

options.text: Run the database on Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server, and install the vendor's agent on the DB instance host.
options.why: RDS Custom gives the agent access to the host, and AWS still automates most of the database administration for the team.

items.explanation: The vendor needs access to the operating system, and the company wants managed administration. RDS Custom automates database administration and lets you [customize your database environment and operating system](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-os-access). AWS says that [Amazon RDS Custom is the better choice](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-vs-rds-vs-ec2) when you need administrative rights to the database and the underlying operating system.
items.takeaway: Host access plus managed administration points to RDS Custom; full control points to EC2.
items.twin: If the stem said "The vendor supports the application on any managed SQL Server database" instead: Amazon RDS for SQL Server, because the agent is not needed and standard RDS leaves less administration to the team.
items.say: The vendor needs the host, so I'd use RDS Custom, which still automates most of the administration.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server: a managed database (automated backups and other automation) that still gives access to the host operating system so the vendor's agent can be installed. Standard RDS gives no OS access; EC2 is fully self-managed.

items.stem: A company runs an encrypted Multi-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the us-east-1 Region. A customer managed AWS KMS key in us-east-1 encrypts the DB instance. A new contract requires cross-Region disaster recovery. If us-east-1 becomes unavailable, the company must run the database in us-west-2 from a copy with a recovery point of minutes, not hours. The copy must stay encrypted at rest. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: a recovery point of minutes, not hours

options.text: Rely on the Multi-AZ standby, because RDS fails over to the standby automatically if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
options.why: RDS places the standby in [a different Availability Zone of the same Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-standby-same-region), so the standby is lost together with us-east-1.

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica of the DB instance in us-west-2, and promote the replica if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
options.why: A DB instance that [replicates asynchronously to a standby DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-region-async-replica-survives-region) in another Region keeps a copy there, and a replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).

options.text: Run MySQL on an Amazon EC2 instance in us-west-2, and manage binary log replication from the DB instance to it.
options.why: It can work, but the team then owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the replication itself.
options.misconception: builds cross-Region replication by hand when RDS has a managed replica

options.text: Choose a KMS key in us-west-2 to encrypt the read replica when the company creates the replica in us-west-2.
options.why: An encrypted replica in another Region needs a key there, so you [specify a KMS key in the destination Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-kms-regional-replica).

options.text: Use the ARN of the KMS key in us-east-1 for the read replica, so that both Regions use one key.
options.why: [KMS keys are specific to the AWS Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-kms-regional-replica) where they are created, so the us-east-1 key cannot encrypt the replica.

items.explanation: Multi-AZ protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption), not against the loss of a Region. A cross-Region read replica is the managed copy in us-west-2. Because the source is encrypted, the company chooses a [KMS key in the destination AWS Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-cross-region-replica-encrypted-source-dest-key) for the replica.
items.takeaway: Region-level recovery needs a cross-Region read replica, encrypted with a KMS key in the destination Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "if one Availability Zone fails" instead: the existing Multi-AZ deployment is enough, because it gives [automatic failover to standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).
items.say: Multi-AZ stays in one Region, so I'd add a cross-Region read replica with a KMS key in us-west-2.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for two steps that together give recovery in another Region with the LEAST operational overhead.

I mark the constraints: an encrypted Multi-AZ DB instance in us-east-1, recovery in us-west-2 if us-east-1 becomes unavailable, a recovery point of minutes, and encryption at rest with a customer managed KMS key.
Before I look at the options, I predict that the Multi-AZ standby already covers this, because RDS fails over to the standby automatically.

I remove the MySQL database on an EC2 instance, because the team would run the database and the replication by hand. I remove the KMS key ARN from us-east-1, because KMS keys are specific to the Region where they are created.

Between the Multi-AZ standby and the cross-Region read replica the difference is the Region. My first idea breaks because the standby is in a different Availability Zone of the same Region, so the standby is lost together with us-east-1. The replica in us-west-2 replicates asynchronously, so its copy is minutes behind, and a replica can be promoted by hand. It needs a KMS key in us-west-2.
Check: the cross-Region read replica and the KMS key in us-west-2 meet every constraint, and nothing extra runs on EC2. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Create a cross-Region read replica in us-west-2 (asynchronous, recovery point of seconds to minutes) and promote it in a disaster. KMS keys are Regional, so an encrypted cross-Region replica must use a KMS key in the destination Region us-west-2.

items.stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance that is encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/rds. RDS takes a daily automated snapshot of the DB instance. A new audit requires that a separate backup account in the same AWS Region receives one copy of the most recent automated snapshot. The backup account must be able to restore the copy. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/rds

options.text: Share the automated snapshot with the backup account directly, so that the backup account can copy it.
options.why: Sharing starts with [copying the automated snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-automated-copy-first) to a manual snapshot, because you can [share manual DB snapshots](../facts/rds.md#rds-snapshots-copy-both-share-manual) and not automated ones.

options.text: Copy the automated snapshot to a manual snapshot under a customer managed key, and allow the backup account to use the key.
options.why: The copy is made [using the customer managed key](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-default-kms-key-not-shareable), and the company can give the backup account access to that key.

options.text: Edit the key policy of the aws/rds key so that the backup account can use the key to decrypt the snapshot.
options.why: You [can't manage, rotate, or delete](../facts/rds.md#rds-kms-aws-managed-key-aws-rds) the aws/rds key, so its key policy stays under the control of AWS.

options.text: Export the database with a dump tool from an Amazon EC2 instance, and upload the dump file to the backup account.
options.why: A dump can work, but the team builds, runs and tests the export and the restore, which snapshot copies do without code.
options.misconception: moves backups with scripts when snapshot copy and sharing do it

options.text: Share the manual snapshot copy with the backup account, so that the backup account can copy the snapshot and restore from it.
options.why: Sharing a manual snapshot [enables authorized AWS accounts to copy the snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-snapshot-copy-or-restore), and the backup account restores from its copy.

items.explanation: Two rules decide this. You can [share manual DB snapshots](../facts/rds.md#rds-snapshots-copy-both-share-manual) and not automated ones, and a snapshot [encrypted using the default KMS key](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-default-kms-key-not-shareable) cannot be shared. So the company copies the snapshot under a customer managed key, gives the backup account access to that key, and shares the copy.
items.takeaway: To share an encrypted automated snapshot, copy it under a customer managed key, then share the manual copy.
items.twin: If the stem said "the DB instance is unencrypted" instead: copy and share the snapshot with no key step, and the account can [directly restore a DB instance from the snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-snapshot-copy-or-restore).
items.say: I'd copy it to a manual snapshot under our own KMS key, then share the key and the copy.

solvers.stem_only: Automated snapshots cannot be shared, and a snapshot encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/rds cannot be shared because that key's policy cannot be changed. So copy the latest automated snapshot to a manual snapshot and re-encrypt it with a customer managed KMS key during the copy; add the backup account to that key's policy; then share the manual snapshot with the backup account, which copies it (or restores from it) using the shared key.

docs/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_RestoreFromSnapshot#You can't restore a DB instance from a D
docs/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ShareSnapshot#Sharing a manual DB snapshot, whether en
docs/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_ShareSnapshot#To share an automated DB snapshot, creat
docs/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/share-encrypted-snapshot#Next you copy the source DB snapshot to

solvers.flag: Option A refers to "the manual snapshot copy", which exists only if D is also chosen, so the wording of A gives away its partner D and the pair cannot be chosen independently; a careful candidate could also defend E if they believe automated snapshots can be shared directly.

items.stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance on a general-purpose instance class. Every afternoon, queries slow down. Amazon CloudWatch shows moderate CPU use, low freeable memory, and read IOPS that are high and keep rising under load. The number of connections is steady and far below the limit. A short outage in the next maintenance window is acceptable. Which change is the MOST operationally efficient way to solve the problem?
keywords: read IOPS that are high and keep rising under load

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, so that the queries use pooled connections and need less memory.
options.why: The proxy can [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share), but connections are steady here, and the queries still read the same data from storage.

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby takes part of the read load.
options.why: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the reads stay on the primary.

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a memory-optimized instance class of a similar size during the next maintenance window.
options.why: A memory-optimized class holds more of the working set in memory, and [you can change your DB instance class](../facts/rds.md#rds-instance-class-changeable) in the maintenance window.

options.text: Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and change the application code to cache the results of the most frequent queries.
options.why: A cache can lower the reads, but developers change the code and the team runs a cache cluster, which a class change avoids.
options.misconception: adds a cache and code changes when the database needs more memory

items.explanation: Low freeable memory and rising read IOPS mean that the working set no longer fits in memory. AWS advises enough RAM so that the working set [resides almost completely in memory](../facts/rds.md#rds-bp-working-set-in-memory). Memory-optimized classes such as db.z1d are [optimized for memory-intensive applications](../facts/rds.md#rds-class-memory-optimized-memory-intensive). The class change makes the database [temporarily unavailable](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-compute-scale-brief-outage) for a short time, which the stem accepts.
items.takeaway: Low freeable memory with rising read IOPS points to a memory-optimized instance class.
items.twin: If the stem said "the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use" instead: RDS Proxy, because it keeps a [smaller number of long-lived connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections).
items.say: The working set no longer fits in memory, so I'd move to a memory-optimized class.

solvers.stem_only: Low freeable memory with high and rising read IOPS means the working set no longer fits in memory and reads go to storage. Scale to a memory-optimized instance class (for example r-class) during the maintenance window. Connections are not the problem, so not RDS Proxy.

items.stem: A company runs an order database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with General Purpose SSD storage. Twice last quarter, the allocated storage filled up, and the application could not write new orders until an engineer added storage. The data grows at an unpredictable rate. The company does not want to pay in advance for a large amount of storage that it does not use. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on free storage space that invokes an AWS Lambda function to increase the allocated storage.
options.why: It works, but the team builds and maintains the alarm and the function, which storage autoscaling does without any code.
options.misconception: builds storage scaling by hand when RDS has it built in

options.text: Allocate twice the current storage now, and reduce the allocated storage again after the company deletes old orders each year.
options.why: Allocated storage cannot shrink, because [you can't deallocate space](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-increase-min-10-percent), so the extra storage stays and the company pays for it.

options.text: Change the storage type to Provisioned IOPS SSD, so that busy write periods no longer fill the allocated storage.
options.why: Provisioned IOPS gives [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production), not more space, so the storage still fills.
options.misconception: confuses storage performance (IOPS) with storage capacity

options.text: Turn on storage autoscaling for the DB instance, and set a maximum storage threshold that fits the company's budget.
options.why: When RDS detects low free space, [it automatically scales up your storage](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable), and the [maximum storage threshold](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-max-threshold) caps the growth.

items.explanation: Storage autoscaling is the RDS feature for this case, and AWS points to it [if your workload is unpredictable](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable). Turning it on [doesn't cause any downtime](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-no-downtime). Storage grows in steps as the data grows, so the company does not pay for a large reserve in advance, and the team does not watch the free space.
items.takeaway: Storage that fills at an unpredictable rate points to storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold.
items.twin: If the stem said "the database needs faster, more consistent storage, not more space" instead: Provisioned IOPS storage, because it gives [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production).
items.say: I'd turn on storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold, so storage grows before it fills.

solvers.stem_only: Turn on RDS storage autoscaling with a maximum storage threshold: RDS grows storage automatically when free space runs low, and you pay only for what is allocated as it grows.

items.stem: A company created an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance for a project that has ended. The DB instance has automated backups with a backup retention period of 7 days. The company will delete the DB instance today to stop paying for it. A regulation requires the company to retain the current data for 2 years, so that the company can restore the data if an auditor asks. What should the company do when it deletes the DB instance?
keywords: retain the current data for 2 years

options.text: Create a final DB snapshot as part of the deletion, and keep the snapshot until the 2 years end.
options.why: [If you take a final snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-final-snapshot-option), you can restore the deleted DB instance from it later.

options.text: Delete the DB instance without a final snapshot, because the automated backups stay available after the deletion.
options.why: Unless the company chooses to retain them, [all automated backups are deleted](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-instance-automated-backups-deleted) with the DB instance.

options.text: Raise the backup retention period of the automated backups to 2 years, and then delete the DB instance.
options.why: The retention period can be set [between 0 and 35 days](../facts/rds.md#rds-backup-retention-range), so automated backups cannot reach 2 years.

options.text: Stop the DB instance instead of deleting it, and start the DB instance again when an auditor asks for the data.
options.why: A DB instance can stay stopped for [7 consecutive days](../facts/rds.md#rds-stop-max-seven-days); after that, RDS starts it again automatically.
options.misconception: a stopped DB instance stays stopped until someone starts it

items.explanation: Snapshots that you take, a final snapshot included, are independent of the DB instance: [Manual snapshots are not deleted](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-instance-automated-backups-deleted) with it. They are [kept until you explicitly delete them](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-snapshots-user-initiated-kept-until-deleted), so the final snapshot holds today's data for the 2 years.
items.takeaway: To keep data after you delete a DB instance, take a final snapshot, which stays until you delete it.
items.twin: If the stem said "restore any second of the last week" instead: a point-in-time restore before the deletion, because RDS can recover to [any point in time](../facts/rds.md#rds-automated-backup-pitr-in-retention) in the retention period.
items.say: I'd take a final snapshot when I delete it; snapshots stay until we delete them.

solvers.stem_only: Create a final DB snapshot at deletion. It is a manual snapshot that stays until deleted, covering 2 years. Automated backups expire with the retention period (maximum 35 days), and a stopped instance restarts automatically after 7 days.

items.stem: A company's web application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to fix a performance problem without any change to the application's SQL queries. Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent at peak, but the number of database connections stays low. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent
the number of database connections stays low

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to use the proxy endpoint.
options.why: The proxy can [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share), but connections are not the problem here, and each read query still runs on the DB instance.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to send its read-only queries to the replica.
options.why: Clients get [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only), which is enough for dashboards, and the read work moves off the primary.

options.text: Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances, and run a connection pooler and streaming read replicas that the team manages.
options.why: Self-managed replicas can take the reads, but on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) of the database.
options.misconception: builds read scaling by hand when RDS read replicas exist

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby instance also serves part of the query load.
options.why: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the CPU load on the primary stays the same.

items.explanation: The load comes from read queries, and the connections are few. A read replica is a [read-only copy of a DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition), made for [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition). The dashboards send their queries to the replica endpoint, and the primary keeps its CPU for the rest of the application.
items.takeaway: High read CPU with few connections points to a read replica, not to RDS Proxy or Multi-AZ.
items.twin: If the stem said "During spiky traffic, thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections, and the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use" instead: RDS Proxy, because it pools [frequent short database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling).
items.say: The reads are the load, so I'd move the dashboard queries to a read replica.

solvers.stem_only: High CPU from read queries with few connections: offload the reads to a read replica and point the read-only connection settings at the replica endpoint. RDS Proxy fixes connection count, not CPU; a Multi-AZ DB instance standby serves no reads.

items.stem: A company is choosing a database engine for a new application on Amazon RDS. The company's reporting team needs a read replica of the production database. On the replica, the team must create its own indexes and summary tables with DDL statements, and the replica must keep receiving all changes from the source DB instance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: create its own indexes and summary tables with DDL statements
keep receiving all changes from the source DB instance

options.text: Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, create a read replica, and make the replica writable for the reporting team's DDL statements.
options.why: AWS does not allow an RDS for PostgreSQL read replica [to be made writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-postgresql-not-writable), so the DDL statements fail.

options.text: Use a Multi-AZ DB cluster of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and run the DDL statements through the reader endpoint of the cluster.
options.why: The reader instances behind the reader endpoint [support only read operations](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-writer-reader-endpoints), so DDL statements there fail.
options.misconception: the readable standbys of a Multi-AZ DB cluster also accept writes

options.text: Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and build a job that copies every change from the DB instance into a separate reporting DB instance.
options.why: A custom copy job works, but developers write, test and run the job, which a writable MySQL replica makes unnecessary.
options.misconception: writes replication code when the engine has a writable replica

options.text: Use Amazon RDS for MySQL, create a read replica, and set the read_only parameter of the replica to 0.
options.why: RDS for MySQL lets you [permit DDL SQL statements against a read replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-read-replica-mysql-ddl) through the read_only parameter, with no code to write.

items.explanation: The deciding need is DDL on a replica that keeps replicating. RDS for MariaDB and MySQL replicas use logical replication, and you can enable a MySQL [read replica to be writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-mysql-logical-writable). After this parameter change on the replica, the team adds its indexes and tables there, and changes from the source keep arriving.
items.takeaway: DDL on a replica that keeps replicating points to RDS for MySQL or MariaDB, not to RDS for PostgreSQL.
items.twin: If the stem said "the team runs only SELECT queries on the replica" instead: either engine fits, because every read replica gives [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only).
items.say: A MySQL replica can take DDL with read_only set to zero; a PostgreSQL replica can't.

solvers.stem_only: Choose RDS for MySQL (or MariaDB): its read replicas can be made writable by setting the read_only parameter to 0 in the replica's parameter group, so the team can add indexes and tables while replication continues. RDS for PostgreSQL read replicas are read-only.
